newsitem.title: CANADA: Alberta economy to lead Canada growth, study says.
newsitem.headline: Alberta economy to lead Canada growth, study says.

text.p: Oil-rich Alberta will benefit from a resource-based economic boom to lead all Canadian provinces in economic growth this year and in 1998, a study released on Tuesday by Canada's largest bank said.

In its latest forecast of the provincial economies, the Royal Bank of Canada said booms in the energy, mining and construction sectors would help Alberta post a 4.1 percent rise in real gross domestic product (GDP) in 1997 and a 4.2 percent increase in 1998.
The study also said that monetary and retail conditions would encourage economic growth in the rest of Canada.
"Low interest rates and modest increases in personal disposable income will enable consumers to keep spending more in all provinces," said Lise Basterache, the bank's assistant chief economist.
The forecast projected Ontario would nip at the heels of Alberta with a 3.3 percent GDP growth rate this year, accelerating to 3.6 percent in 1998.

Prince Edward Island will post the worst growth rate in 1997 at -0.4 percent, mostly because the island province's economy was artificially boosted last year by construction of the Confederation Bridge to the mainland, the bank said.
Across Canada, total gross domestic product is expected to increase by 3.0 percent in 1997 and 3.1 percent in 1998, the bank said.
But the bank cautioned that economic growth would not be enough to force a breakthrough on Canada's unemployment front.

"For most provinces, despite stronger job growth this year, unemployment rates are not expected to decline as job gains will be matched by new entrants to the labor force," said Carlos Leitao, an economist with the bank.
"Saskatchewan will continue to have the lowest unemployment rate in Canada followed by Alberta, Manitoba and British Columbia," Leitao added.
